The method provides gaze-adaptive rendering by predicting where a user is likely to look within an image or a sequence of images. One or more images are analyzed to identify image-related features that may attract or guide visual attention, such as objects, motion, contrast, color, edges, depth, or other salient content. Based on this analysis, the method determines a predicted future point of regard representing a location at which the user is expected to direct their gaze at a subsequent time.

An area surrounding the predicted point of regard is then defined. The size, shape, and position of this area may be selected according to the prediction, the characteristics of the display, the type of content, or a desired level of visual quality. The area may also be updated over time as new images are received and the predicted point of regard changes.

When the image stream is displayed, at least one image-characteristic parameter is assigned a first value within the area surrounding the predicted point of regard and a different value outside that area. The parameter may relate, for example, to spatial resolution, sharpness, contrast, brightness, color precision, frame rate, compression, sampling density, or rendering quality. In one implementation, the predicted viewing region is rendered at a higher quality, while peripheral regions are rendered with reduced detail or lower resource requirements. Transitions between the regions may be gradual to reduce visible boundaries or artifacts.

By concentrating display and processing resources on the portion of the image that the user is expected to view, the method can preserve perceived image quality while reducing the resources devoted to less visually important regions. This approach may decrease computational load, memory bandwidth, transmission bandwidth, power consumption, or rendering latency. The technique can be applied to displays, video systems, virtual- or augmented-reality devices, remote rendering platforms, and other systems that present image streams to a user.
outputs.L5:
### Method, POR, and PORn

In software verification, **Partial Order Reduction (POR)** is a method used to limit the number of states that must be explored when analyzing concurrent systems. Such systems often contain many independent operations whose different execution orders lead to equivalent results. POR identifies these operations and examines only representative sequences, reducing computational effort without losing relevant behaviors.

**PORn** can be understood as a parameterized or extended form of POR, where *n* specifies the reduction depth, number of processes, or another method-dependent parameter. This extension enables the reduction strategy to be adapted to the size and complexity of a particular system.

The effectiveness of any POR or PORn method depends on correctly identifying dependencies between operations. A well-designed method can significantly improve verification speed and memory usage while preserving important properties such as safety, reachability, and deadlock detection.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent abstract for a gaze-contingent image display method that predicts a user’s future point of regard using image analysis and applies different image parameter values inside and outside the gaze region.
counterfactuals.output: A gaze-contingent image display method includes receiving image data for presentation on a display and analyzing the image data to identify one or more image features indicative of a likely future point of regard of a user. A predicted point of regard is determined based at least in part on the identified image features and, optionally, current or historical gaze data. A gaze region is defined relative to the predicted point of regard. The image data is rendered using a first value of an image parameter within the gaze region and a second, different value of the image parameter outside the gaze region. The image parameter may include resolution, sampling rate, sharpness, contrast, brightness, color, compression level, frame rate, or rendering quality. The predicted point of regard and gaze region may be updated dynamically as image content or gaze information changes, thereby improving perceived image quality while reducing computational, bandwidth, or power requirements.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate formal patent-style language for a method that analyzes upcoming video frames to predict where a viewer will look and selectively adjusts image quality in the predicted area of attention.
counterfactuals.output:
### Exemplary Method Claim

1. **A computer-implemented method for adaptive rendering of video content, the method comprising:**

   receiving, by one or more processors, a sequence of video frames for presentation to a viewer;

   accessing at least one upcoming video frame that is temporally subsequent to a video frame currently being presented;

   analyzing the at least one upcoming video frame to identify one or more visual features associated with predicted viewer attention;

   determining, based at least in part on the one or more visual features, a predicted region of attention within a display area for a future presentation time;

   generating a spatially varying quality allocation for the at least one upcoming video frame, the spatially varying quality allocation assigning a first image-quality level to the predicted region of attention and a second image-quality level to a region outside the predicted region of attention, wherein the first image-quality level is greater than the second image-quality level;

   processing the at least one upcoming video frame in accordance with the spatially varying quality allocation; and

   causing the processed upcoming video frame to be presented to the viewer at the future presentation time.

2. **The method of claim 1**, wherein analyzing the at least one upcoming video frame comprises detecting at least one of an object, a face, text, motion, a scene transition, a contrast feature, a depth discontinuity, or a salient visual event.

3. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising obtaining gaze data indicative of a current or historical gaze direction of the viewer, wherein determining the predicted region of attention is further based on the gaze data.

4. **The method of claim 3**, wherein the gaze data is obtained from at least one of an eye-tracking sensor, a head-tracking sensor, an orientation sensor, a camera, or a user-interaction device.

5. **The method of claim 1**, wherein determining the predicted region of attention comprises applying a trained machine-learning model to data representing a plurality of upcoming video frames.

6. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the predicted region of attention includes a first portion corresponding to a predicted gaze location and at least one peripheral portion surrounding the first portion, and wherein the spatially varying quality allocation specifies progressively reduced image quality as a distance from the predicted gaze location increases.

7. **The method of claim 1**, wherein adjusting image quality comprises varying at least one of spatial resolution, temporal resolution, quantization level, compression ratio, bitrate, chroma resolution, bit depth, sampling density, sharpening, denoising, texture detail, or rendering fidelity.

8. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising determining a confidence value associated with the predicted region of attention and adjusting at least one of a size, shape, location, or image-quality level of the predicted region based on the confidence value.

9. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the at least one upcoming video frame comprises a plurality of temporally ordered upcoming video frames, and wherein determining the predicted region of attention comprises predicting a trajectory of viewer attention across the plurality of temporally ordered upcoming video frames.

10. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the spatially varying quality allocation is generated subject to at least one resource constraint comprising a bandwidth constraint, a processing constraint, a power constraint, a memory constraint, or a latency constraint.

11. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising comparing an observed gaze location with the predicted region of attention and updating a prediction model based on a difference between the observed gaze location and the predicted region of attention.

12. **The method of claim 1**, wherein processing the at least one upcoming video frame comprises selectively encoding, transmitting, decoding, rendering, or enhancing the predicted region of attention at the first image-quality level.

### Exemplary System Claim

13. **A system for adaptive presentation of video content, comprising:**

   a memory storing instructions; and

   one or more processors configured, upon execution of the instructions, to:

   obtain video data representing a plurality of video frames, including an upcoming video frame;

   analyze image content of the upcoming video frame before presentation of the upcoming video frame;

   predict, from the analyzed image content, a spatial region at which viewer attention is expected to be directed during presentation of the upcoming video frame;

   allocate a greater amount of image-processing or transmission resources to the spatial region than to at least one other spatial region of the upcoming video frame; and

   cause presentation of the upcoming video frame with selectively increased image quality in the spatial region.

### Exemplary Specification Language

In some implementations, a look-ahead attention-prediction engine analyzes one or more frames positioned ahead of a current playback position. The engine may identify spatial and temporal characteristics likely to attract viewer attention, including object motion, faces, text, luminance changes, scene cuts, semantic importance, and visual saliency. Based on such characteristics, optionally together with current or historical gaze information, the engine generates an attention map representing respective probabilities that portions of a subsequently presented frame will be viewed.

A quality-allocation engine may use the attention map to assign nonuniform image-quality levels across the subsequently presented frame. A region having a relatively high predicted attention probability may be encoded, transmitted, decoded, rendered, or enhanced using a higher quality setting, while one or more regions having lower predicted attention probabilities may be processed using reduced quality settings. The allocation may thereby reduce computational load, bandwidth consumption, power consumption, or rendering latency while maintaining perceived image quality in an area expected to receive viewer attention.
